newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sunni Moslem militants call strike in Karachi.
newsitem.headline: Sunni Moslem militants call strike in Karachi.

text.p: A militant Sunni Moslem group on Monday called a strike in Karachi in protest against a bomb blast that killed its leader and 25 other people.
A spokesman for Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) said the organisation wanted transport and business in the southern port city, Pakistan's commercial hub, to shut down on Tuesday.
The strike call was in response to the death of SSP chief Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi, who was among 26 people killed in Saturday's explosion outside a courthouse in Lahore.

Deputy SSP leader Azam Tariq, one of about 90 people wounded in the blast, was released on parole from a Lahore hospital to attend the funeral prayers of his mother, who died of shock in Chichawatni on Sunday, newspapers reported.
The bomb exploded as Faruqi and Tariq were being brought to the Sessions Court in Lahore, where they were due to appear on charges of involvement in murdering several Shi'ite Moslems.
The English-language daily The News said a suspect arrested by a policeman at the scene of the blast had confessed to setting off the remote-control device.

It quoted police sources as saying that Mehram Ali had told investigators that a Shi'ite leader had told him to sit on a parked motorcycle until the SSP leaders arrived at the court and push a button to activate what he was told was a tape recorder.
"However, when I saw a huge police force accompanying the SSP leaders, I got nervous and went to the corridor from where I pushed the button," Mehram was quoted as saying.

The News said Mehram had been arrested in 1990 and sentenced to 10 years in jail for possessing hand grenades. His term was reduced to seven years by a higher court and he was finally released by the Supreme Court after four years.
On Sunday, SSP activists sacked and burned the Iranian cultural centre in Lahore. drawing a protest from Iran.
The Iranian Embassy in Islamabad condemned the attack and asked Pakistan to arrest the perpetrators, Iranian radio said.

The bombing, which Sunni hardliners blame on Iran and the local Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) group, has raised fears of sectarian unrest just two weeks before Pakistani elections. The TJP has condemned the blast.

No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. It appeared to be the latest in a long-running feud between militants in Pakistan's majority Sunni and minority Shi'ite communities, which cost about 170 lives last year.
Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's population of over 130 million, but are a majority in neighbouring Iran.
